newsitem.title: UK: End of Belgian Central Bank sales a plus for gold.
newsitem.headline: End of Belgian Central Bank sales a plus for gold.

text.p: The bullion market should be encouraged by news that Belgium was finished selling gold reserves and that G-10 central bankers coordinated closely with each other on such sales, market analysts said on Monday.
But they disagreed as to just how bullish the news was.
Gold prices edged up just $0.40 Monday, and closed at $380.40/90 in trading which was especially quiet due to the Columbus Day holiday in the U.S.

Alan Baker, chairman of London Bullion Market Association, noted that the amount of Belgian gold sales had been small compared to the volume of officially-held gold reserves, and had never disturbed the market.
"The amount the Belgians sold hardly scratches the surface -- 700 tonnes out of 35,000 tonnes," Baker said.
"If it's been re-emphasised that the Group of 10 have some formal agreement not to destabilise the price, that is encouraging to the market," Baker said. "But it's not earthshattering."

Belgian Central Bank chairman Alfons Verplaetse said in a newspaper interview that G-10 central bankers had an accord not to destabilise the gold market and to ask each other for permission in the case of planned sales.
Verplaetse also said Belgium's reserves were in line with the European average after selling 700 tonnes, adding that he would not be seeking permission again.
"These sorts of things do help to some extent. They definitively said they are not contemplating any more sales," said Helen Junz of the World Gold Council.
"But the amounts have not been great and they have not disturbed the market. It gives reassurance, but you'll have to see to what extent the market reacts."
One analyst said the news was bullish at face value and likely to spark a price move higher as it reduced the fear of above-ground stocks leaking into the market and depressing the price of gold.
"What is the best possible news the market could get? This is it. I think we can move up on this," the analyst said.

None of the analysts polled were aware of a policy by the central banks of the G-10 -- the U.S., Germany, Japan, Canada, the U.K. France, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Sweden -- requiring permission for planned sales.
A Bank of England spokeswoman said officials were unavailable for comment.
"It was known that (central banks) were always interested in that the markets are not disturbed and that central banks talk to each other," Junz said.
